one_liner: Rust find-and-replace CLI (regex crate, JS/Python-style syntax); several times faster than GNU sed on regex-heavy substitutions.
what_it_does: sd replaces every match of a regex (or, with -F, a literal string) with a replacement that may use $1 or ${name} captures, reading stdin or a list of files. Giving file arguments rewrites them in place through a temp file plus rename; -p previews to stdout instead. It is not a sed replacement: one find/replace pair per run, no addresses, hold space, scripts or multiple expressions. Unreleased master (February 2026) processes input line by line by default and needs -A/--across for whole-file (multi-line) matching; the released 1.0.0 always works on whole files.
how_it_is_fast: Matching is done by the Rust regex crate (regex::bytes, 1.10.2 in Cargo.lock), a finite-automata engine with worst-case O(m*n) search that omits backreferences and look-around, while GNU sed uses glibc's POSIX regex engine; the large regex gaps are an engine-against-engine difference whose size also depends on sed's locale, which no benchmark states. Replacement is one pass appending into a single output buffer and returns the input borrowed when nothing matches. With -A each input is read whole and multiple files are replaced in parallel with rayon; the default mode reads 8 KB chunks and runs the regex once per line, which the README puts at about 2-3x slower than -A.
when_to_use: Ad hoc or scripted single substitutions where you want PCRE/JavaScript-style regex (\d, \w, (?P<name>...), $1) without sed's escaping, delimiter and BRE/ERE rules.

Regex-heavy rewrites with classes and capture groups on large text or JSON files, where the Rust regex engine beats GNU sed's glibc regex (independent 2019 run: about 3x on a 120 MB JSON with (\w+) -> $1$1).
Literal or regex replacement across many files with -A (master) or the released 1.0.0, which process files in parallel with rayon and write each file atomically via a temp file and rename.
Streaming stdin (for example journalctl -f | sd ...) with bounded memory on master's default line-by-line mode (README: 3 MB peak RSS vs 74 MB for -A on a 36 MB file).
when_not_to_use: Anything beyond one s///g: sed addresses and ranges, hold space, multiple -e expressions, delete/insert commands, or existing scripts that rely on POSIX BRE/ERE syntax.
Patterns that need backreferences or look-around; the Rust regex crate does not implement them.

Plain literal substitutions piped through stdout in the default line-by-line mode: the README table has sd 357.0 ms vs sed 316.4 ms on 1M lines, and every output line is a separate write(2) because Rust's stdout is line-buffered even when redirected.

Many large files with -A on master: all inputs are read fully into memory and all replaced outputs are held before any file is written; the released 1.0.0 maps whole files (memory issues #96 and #154 were only closed by unreleased #328).
When you need the behaviour the README documents from a package: crates.io and distributions ship 1.0.0 (2023-11-08), which has no line-by-line mode and no -A flag.

integration.form: crate (CLI binary installed with cargo install sd; master also splits out an sd library crate and an unpublished sd-cli binary crate)
integration.dependencies: regex 1.10, rayon 1.8, thiserror, tempfile; clap 4.4 for the CLI (released 1.0.0 also uses memmap2)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.86, edition 2024 on master; Rust 1.70 for the released 1.0.0
integration.platforms: any Rust target; Windows supported since 0.5.0; master adds aarch64 Linux and Windows ARM64 release builds
integration.thread_safety: CLI tool; with -A (and in 1.0.0 in-place mode) files are processed in parallel by rayon; library thread-safety not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — covers only sed's s/find/replace/g, with different regex syntax ($1 instead of \1, no backreferences in patterns) and in-place editing whenever files are given (sed needs -i)

gotchas: Harness flaw: the README's 11.93x regex row is invalid as printed. hyperfine runs each command through sh -c, so the double-quoted "$1$1" expands to an empty string and sd deleted every word while sed doubled every word (open issue #52 since 2019). The measured 2018 code (324fd1c) also ran the unescape crate over each whole output, decoding JSON escapes such as \" and \n that sed left alone (fixed in 0.4.2). With correct quoting, an independent 2019 run (sd -p, 120 MB, MacBook Pro 2015 i5) measured 12.6 s vs GNU sed 37.5-39.3 s, about 3x.

The README's line-by-line table (default sd 357.0 ms, slower than sed) was measured at commit c79546a, before the chunked-read commit fcdb8b3 in the same PR, whose message reports 106 ms vs sed 120 ms and 33 ms for -A from a different run; the README was never updated. The 0.997 s for ~1.5 GB of JSON is hard to reconcile with the 2018 code, which copied every output into a VecDeque<char> for the unescape pass (an inference, not reproduced). Re-running the README commands with current sd edits the inputs in place, and the $1$1 command empties every word of dump.json on its first warmup.

Default line-by-line mode changes semantics: -n LIMIT applies per line although --help says per file (the limit tests all pass -A), \n and other multi-line patterns need -A, and -f w rebuilds the regex builder, dropping flags given before it (for example -f iw loses case-insensitivity) and multi-line mode.

On master, in-place writes no longer keep the file owner: the fchown code from #326 sits in sd/src/output.rs, which lib.rs never declares as a module, so the CHANGELOG entry does not apply to the compiled binary.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick sd over RustyBox's sed applet or awkrs when the job is one regex or literal substitution and you want Rust regex syntax rather than sed or awk compatibility; inside a Rust program use the regex crate (catalogued separately), the engine sd wraps, directly.
verified_claims_summary: The README's large-file tables are 2018 hyperfine runs of sd 0.4.0-era code (commit 324fd1c) against GNU sed with no hardware, sed version or locale: 0.997 s vs 2.338 s on ~1.5 GB of JSON and 0.942 s vs 11.3 s on a 55 MB JSON, the latter with sd's replacement shell-expanded to an empty string. The only independent figure found (issue #52, 2019, MacBook Pro 2015 i5, 120 MB) is about 3x faster than GNU sed, and the 2026 1M-line table has -A mode 2.5x faster than sed on a literal while the default mode was slower at the time.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-02-25) and MIT-licensed, but the README documents unreleased master while crates.io and distributions ship 1.0.0 from 2023, and its headline 11.93x regex row is invalid as printed (shell-expanded $1$1 made sd delete words while sed doubled them, open issue #52), with an independent rerun showing about 3x.
